subtitle: Read Minnesota's goals for employing people with disabilities accurately, interpret self-identified counts with their limits in view, and lead the retention, advancement and accommodation systems that decide whether those goals are met.
audience: For DHS and DSD supervisors, managers and program leaders who hire, supervise, budget for or report on staff, and who want to understand the state's disability employment goals beyond a single hiring pathway.

lessons.title: What the state's goal says, and how long it lasts
objectives: Describe Minnesota's goal for employing people with disabilities as Executive Order 19-15 states it, including who it directs and what it asks of agencies.
Explain why an executive order's goal must be checked for current status before it is cited.
Distinguish duties in Minnesota Statutes section 43A.191 that do not depend on the order.
Explain why an enterprise goal is not a rule for an individual hiring decision.
lessons.teaching:
Minnesota's goal for employing people with disabilities in state service comes from an executive order, and a leader should know what it says before repeating it. Executive Order 19-15, "Providing for Increased State Employment of Individuals with Disabilities," was signed on April 1, 2019. It directs Minnesota Management and Budget (MMB) to work toward a goal of 10 percent employment of people with disabilities in the executive branch, and it rescinded the earlier Executive Order 14-14. The order notes that the share of agency employees who self-identified as having a disability rose from 4 percent in 2013 to more than 7 percent in 2018. Those are the order's figures at its signing, not a current count.

The order assigns work at two levels. MMB was to build a plan that includes accessible training for hiring managers, HR staff, affirmative action officers and ADA coordinators, set up quarterly reporting to the Governor, post enterprise-wide statistics on hiring and turnover to the extent the law permits, and develop a procedure for consulting MMB before an accommodation is denied for lack of funding. Each agency is to use its best efforts toward its affirmative action goals and accessibility standards, develop its own plan with recruitment and training programs in consultation with MMB, use the on-the-job demonstration process where the law permits, consult the Chief Information Accessibility Officer before buying new technology, and evaluate its own compliance from time to time. The order also states that it does not require any employee to disclose disability status involuntarily.

An executive order does not last indefinitely, which matters for anyone quoting the 10 percent figure. Under Minnesota Statutes section 4.035, subdivision 3, an executive order expires 90 days after the governor who issued it leaves office, unless a statute or the order sets an earlier date or it is rescinded sooner. A new administration may continue an order, replace it or let it lapse. Before you cite the goal in a plan, a briefing or a team conversation, confirm with Human Resources or the agency's affirmative action officer whether Executive Order 19-15 is still in effect or has been replaced, and what the current target is.

Some duties do not depend on the order at all. Minnesota Statutes section 43A.191 requires each executive branch agency's affirmative action plan to include a reasonable accommodation program for hiring and promoting people with disabilities and a section that ensures hiring, placement and advancement opportunities at all levels, and it requires agencies to identify positions suited to supported employment. Connect 700, the on-the-job demonstration pathway, has its own course; this one looks at the system around it. Read the goal for what it is: an aggregate target for the executive branch that guides recruitment, access and retention. It is not a rule for an individual hiring decision, and it gives no one a reason to ask a colleague whether they have a disability. Formal decisions about hiring, accommodation and civil rights stay with Human Resources, the ADA coordinator and the Equal Opportunity and Access Division; this course helps you understand and support that work.
lessons.keyPoint: Executive Order 19-15 set an executive-branch goal of 10 percent employment of people with disabilities, but an order's life is tied to the governor who issued it. Confirm its current status before citing it, and remember that the statutory plan duties stand on their own.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} is drafting a division workforce update and copies a line from an older slide deck: "DHS must reach 10 percent employees with disabilities by the end of next year." {{SUPERVISOR}}, reviewing the draft, cannot find where the deadline came from and notices that the slide is several years old.
lessons.question: What should {{SUPERVISOR}} suggest before the update goes out?
choices: Keep the line as written, since a firm deadline gives managers a clear reason to recruit more actively.
Check the line against the order and current HR guidance, then describe it as an enterprise goal.
Remove every mention of the goal, so the update cannot be read as pressure on current staff.
feedback: A deadline that the order does not state, attached to an agency rather than the executive branch, could mislead managers and push them toward pressuring individuals. Accuracy matters more than urgency here.

This keeps the goal in the update while making it accurate. It names the source, describes the goal at the level the order sets it and confirms with Human Resources whether the order is still current.

Silence avoids one risk but loses useful context. Leaders can discuss an accurate goal without pressuring anyone, as long as they describe it as a target for systems rather than a question for individuals.
lessons.reflection: Privately recall the last time you heard a workforce goal stated at work, or use the slide in the practice case. Did anyone say where the figure came from, when it was set or whether it still applied? What would make it easier for you to ask?
lessons.action: Find one place your unit cites a disability employment figure or goal, such as a slide, plan or report. Note its source and date, then ask Human Resources or the affirmative action officer whether it reflects the current order and target. Revise or retire it based on the answer.

check.question: Why should a leader confirm the status of Executive Order 19-15 before citing its goal?
check.correct: An executive order expires after the governor who issued it leaves office, unless it ends sooner, and it may be replaced.
wrong: Executive orders must be re-signed by the Legislature every two years in order to stay in force.
The goal applies only to agencies that have already met it, so its status changes every quarter.
check.feedback: Minnesota Statutes section 4.035, subdivision 3, ties an order's life to the governor who issued it: it expires 90 days after that governor leaves office unless an earlier end applies. The Legislature does not re-sign orders, and the goal does not depend on whether an agency has met it.

lessons.title: Self-identification and why the count is uncertain
objectives: Explain how disability counts in state employment are produced through voluntary self-identification.
Describe the conditions federal guidance sets on inviting employees to self-identify.
Identify reasons a reported percentage can rise, fall or stay flat without a change in hiring.
Plan a team message about self-identification that is general, voluntary and free of pressure.
lessons.teaching:
Every figure about state employees with disabilities rests on people choosing to tell their employer. MMB's guide to Self Service, dated January 2024, describes a Voluntary Self-Identification of Disability page where employees can add or change their status. It explains that the information is used to determine whether the state has a diverse workforce, and it states that employees are not legally required to provide it. Applicants are asked separately, and answering is optional there too. Executive Order 19-15 adds that nothing in it requires anyone to disclose disability status involuntarily.

Federal guidance sets conditions on asking. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's 2000 enforcement guidance on disability-related inquiries of employees says an employer may invite voluntary self-identification when it is carrying out affirmative action required by law or voluntarily using the information to benefit people with disabilities. The invitation must state clearly that the information is for that purpose, that giving it is voluntary, that it will be kept confidential, that refusing will bring no adverse treatment and that it will be used only in line with the ADA. A leader's part is therefore narrow: explain why the state asks, point to the official process and accept any answer, including no answer at all.

Because the count depends on disclosure, it is uncertain in predictable ways. Some employees acquire a disability after they are hired and never update their record. Some decide disclosure is not worth the risk, especially if they have seen colleagues treated differently after asking for help. Others do not think of a chronic illness, a mental health condition or a gradual hearing change as a disability, and some choose to decline. A rise in the reported share can mean that more people with disabilities were hired, that more current employees updated their status, or both. A flat number can hide new hires offset by departures. Read any change with those possibilities in view, and ask the person who owns the data what it can and cannot support.

The leadership question, then, is not how to raise the count but whether people would feel safe being counted. That trust is built by how accommodation requests are handled, by how disability comes up in ordinary conversation and by what happens after someone discloses. Never guess who has a disability, ask a particular person to self-identify, or treat accommodation paperwork as a source of demographic data; under MMB Policy 1433, medical information gathered for an accommodation is confidential and kept apart from personnel records. Small units raise a second risk, because a count from a group of a few people can point to individuals. Ask the affirmative action officer or Human Resources how data is summarized and shared before you discuss unit-level figures, and keep any reminder about self-identification general, voluntary and addressed to everyone.
lessons.keyPoint: Disability counts measure who chose to disclose, not everyone with a disability. A leader's job is to make disclosure safe and voluntary, never to raise the count by asking, guessing or using accommodation records.
lessons.example: Practice case: A division report shows that the share of DSD staff who self-identify as having a disability dropped slightly over the past year. {{SUPERVISOR}} wonders aloud in a leadership meeting whether supervisors should ask employees they know have accommodations to update their Self Service records. {{CASE_MANAGER}}, a lead worker attending to present a project, is unsure whether to speak up.
lessons.question: What is the strongest response to the idea raised in the meeting?
choices: Agree to ask only the employees who already disclosed to their supervisor, since they are comfortable discussing it.
Suggest checking the accommodation files first, so supervisors know whom to remind without raising the subject.
Say that targeting individuals or using accommodation files is off limits, and suggest a general reminder.
feedback: Telling a supervisor about a need is not consent to be asked about self-identification. A targeted request from a supervisor can feel like pressure, however gently it is made.
Accommodation and medical information is confidential and kept apart from personnel records. Using it to target reminders would misuse it and could damage trust in the accommodation process.

This protects both the people and the data. A general reminder that explains the purpose, says answering is optional and goes to everyone keeps disclosure voluntary, and the drop itself can be explored with whoever owns the data.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider what would make someone on your team feel safe enough to self-identify, or what might make them decide not to. You do not need to know anyone's status to think about this. What does your own behavior signal?
lessons.action: Draft a two- or three-sentence reminder about voluntary self-identification that could go to an entire team. Say why the state asks, that answering is optional and that there is no penalty for declining. Ask Human Resources to review it before anyone uses it.

check.question: A unit's reported disability percentage rose this year. What can a leader conclude from that alone?
check.correct: Not much yet: the rise could reflect new hires, more current employees updating their status, or both.
wrong: The unit hired more people with disabilities than it did the previous year.
The unit's accommodation process has improved enough to meet the state goal.
check.feedback: Self-identified counts change when people disclose or update records, not only when hiring changes. A rise is a reason to ask what the data can support, not proof of better hiring or better accommodation.

lessons.title: Retention and advancement: where goals are kept or lost
objectives: Explain why turnover and advancement are part of a disability employment goal.
Distinguish departures that reflect ordinary life changes from those that may reflect workplace barriers, without assuming either.
Examine whether development opportunities on a team are visible and accessible.
Identify what a leader answers for in retention and what belongs to other areas.
lessons.teaching:
A hiring goal can be met at the front door and lost through the back. Executive Order 19-15 directs MMB to post enterprise-wide statistics on both the hiring and the turnover of people with disabilities, to the extent permitted by law, and Minnesota Statutes section 43A.191 requires agency plans to ensure hiring, placement and advancement opportunities for people with disabilities at all levels. When an agency does not meet its hiring goals, the same statute expects a coordinated retention plan alongside active recruitment. Retention and advancement are part of the goal, not a separate topic to take up later.

Why people leave is rarely visible in a count. An employee may leave for a better offer, a move, a change in health or retirement, and none of those is a failure of the workplace. An employee may also leave after months of waiting for an accommodation, after a new supervisor ended an arrangement that worked, after being passed over for development or after hearing comments about disability that no one challenged. Those departures say something about the organization. A leader cannot tell which is which by assuming. They learn through stay conversations offered to everyone on the team, through exit information that Human Resources gathers and through patterns the person responsible for workforce data can share in summary form.

Advancement deserves the same attention. Look at who receives stretch assignments, acting roles, training seats and visible projects, and whether those opportunities are announced or handed out informally. Check whether development itself is accessible: a leadership program with inaccessible materials, a travel requirement with no accommodation route or an exercise that measures speed when the job does not can screen people out long before a promotion decision. Ask whether the criteria for moving up describe the work or describe a familiar way of doing it. Where the agency has job-related criteria, use them consistently; where a process seems to block access, raise it with Human Resources rather than working around it for one person.

Transitions are where working arrangements most often break: a new supervisor, a reorganization, a new system or a return from leave. Another course covers carrying accommodations through those changes in detail; the point here is accountability. A leader answers for whether the people they supervise have what they need to do the work, whether opportunities on the team are visible and fairly shared and whether concerns are acted on promptly. A leader does not answer for anyone's medical details and should not try to learn them. When an employee raises possible disability discrimination or harassment, route it promptly through the established channel to Human Resources or the Equal Opportunity and Access Division, separately from any conversation about staying.
lessons.keyPoint: A goal met through hiring can be lost through departures and stalled careers. Leaders keep the goal by making work, development and transitions accessible, and by learning from departures without guessing at anyone's reasons.
lessons.example: Practice case: Over two years, three staff in a DSD section who had self-identified as having a disability left within eighteen months of starting. {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} learns this from a summary that Human Resources prepared for a leadership retreat, which lists no names. A colleague at the retreat says turnover is normal everywhere and the section should focus on hiring.
lessons.question: How should {{PROGRAM_MANAGER}} respond?
choices: Ask HR what the summary can show, and check whether the section's transitions and development are accessible.
Agree to focus on hiring, because three departures over two years is too small a number to show anything.
Contact the three former employees directly to ask whether their disability was part of why they left the section.
feedback: This takes the pattern seriously without overstating it. It asks what the data can show and examines processes the section controls, such as transitions, development and accommodation follow-through.
Small numbers do call for caution, but caution means looking carefully rather than looking away. Hiring alone will not hold a goal if people continue to leave early.
Contacting former staff about their disability intrudes on private information and puts them in an uncomfortable position. Exit information is gathered by Human Resources through its own process.
lessons.reflection: Privately think about the last opportunity on your team, such as a stretch project or acting role. How was it offered, and could everyone on the team have used it, including someone who needs materials in another format or a different schedule?
lessons.action: List the development opportunities your team offered in the past six months. For each, note how it was announced, what it required and whether an accommodation route was clear. Bring one improvement to your next planning conversation with your manager or Human Resources.

check.question: Which retention step belongs to the leader rather than to Human Resources or the ADA coordinator?
check.correct: Making sure opportunities on the team are announced openly and can be used by everyone who is eligible.
wrong: Deciding whether a former employee's departure was caused by disability discrimination.
Reviewing a departing employee's medical information to understand their reasons for leaving.
check.feedback: Leaders own how work and opportunity are shared on their teams. Findings about discrimination belong to the people and areas that make formal determinations, and leaders should not see or seek medical information.

lessons.title: Accommodation as a system, and what a leader answers for
objectives: Describe how MMB Policy 1433 divides accommodation responsibilities among supervisors, ADA coordinators and MMB.
Explain how the state accommodation account and agency budgeting affect whether accommodations are provided promptly.
Identify system signals a leader can monitor, such as delays and reimbursement use, without seeing private information.
State what a leader answers for in accommodation and what belongs to the ADA coordinator or Human Resources.
lessons.teaching:
An accommodation is decided for one person, but whether accommodations work across an agency is a system question. MMB Policy 1433, ADA Reasonable Accommodation, last revised in 2017, makes the agency ADA coordinator the decision maker for requests outside a supervisor's or manager's authority and leaves each agency to set which low-cost items supervisors may approve. Supervisors do not request medical information; the ADA coordinator does, and that information is kept confidential and separate from personnel records. When an approved accommodation cannot be provided within a reasonable time, the requester is to be updated before the end of 30 days, with temporary measures used where feasible.

Money is where systems fail quietly. The policy requires an agency to consult the State ADA Coordinator at MMB before denying a request for lack of financial resources, and each agency must say how it will pay for accommodations. Minnesota Statutes section 16B.4805 creates an accommodation account from which the commissioner of administration reimburses state agencies up to 50 percent of eligible costs, to the extent funds are available. Eligible costs include accommodations for applicants, ongoing or periodic services and one-time expenses of more than $500 for an employee in a fiscal year. Agency affirmative action plans must track the number of accommodation requests, approvals and reimbursements from that account. These figures have changed over the years, so check the current statute and your agency's procedure before relying on them.

For a leader, the practical rule is that cost should never stand between a person and a working accommodation. A unit with no budget line for accommodation, or a manager who signals that requests are a burden, teaches staff not to ask. That lesson shows up later as quiet departures and low self-identification, which then look like a recruitment problem. Plan for accommodation in the budget, learn your agency's route for reimbursement and keep the conversation with the employee about the work rather than the price. Prevention matters as well: Executive Order 19-15 asks agencies to consult the Chief Information Accessibility Officer before buying new technology, because an inaccessible system turns into a steady stream of individual requests.

Accountability is the thread through this course. A leader answers for routing requests promptly, following up when a promised accommodation is late, budgeting for access, choosing accessible tools and meetings, sharing opportunity fairly and keeping disclosure safe. A leader may also ask for summary information that shows how the system is working: how long requests take, where they stall and how often reimbursement is sought. A leader does not answer for decisions that belong to the ADA coordinator, Human Resources or the affirmative action officer, and should not make those decisions informally. Owning what is yours and routing what is not is how a percentage goal becomes a workplace people choose to stay in.
lessons.keyPoint: Accommodation succeeds or fails as a system of routing, timing, budgeting and prevention. Leaders answer for that system in their area and route individual decisions to the ADA coordinator and Human Resources.
lessons.example: Practice case: {{SUPERVISOR}} approves a new team member's request for a screen reader-compatible version of a case tracking tool, and the ADA coordinator agrees an accommodation is needed. Five weeks later nothing has arrived. The team's budget is tight, and a manager mentions that the unit may have to wait for next fiscal year.
lessons.question: What should {{SUPERVISOR}} do now?
choices: Tell the team member the request is on hold until next fiscal year, since the budget decision is out of the unit's hands.
Follow up with the ADA coordinator, ask about interim measures and reimbursement, and raise the delay with the manager.
Ask the team member to manage with a coworker's help for now, so the unit can avoid the cost this year.
feedback: Budget pressure is real, but a funding shortfall is not the unit's decision to make alone. Under statewide policy, MMB is consulted before a request is denied for lack of resources, and the person should already have received an update.

This keeps the person informed and the process moving. It asks about temporary measures, the accommodation account and the required consultation before any funding-based delay becomes a denial, and it brings the system problem to the manager.
An informal workaround can shift work onto a colleague and leave the person dependent on someone else. It also sidesteps the formal process rather than resolving the delay.
lessons.reflection: Privately consider what your team would conclude if it watched how the last accommodation request in your area was handled, or the one in the practice case. Would they feel more or less willing to ask for what they need?
lessons.action: Ask your manager or budget lead how your unit plans for accommodation costs and how reimbursement from the state accommodation account is requested. Then ask the ADA coordinator what summary information about request timelines could help you spot delays in your area.

check.question: Under MMB Policy 1433, what must happen before an agency denies an accommodation request for lack of financial resources?
check.correct: The agency must consult the State ADA Coordinator at Minnesota Management and Budget.
wrong: The supervisor must document that the team cannot absorb the cost this fiscal year.
The employee must first apply for reimbursement from the state accommodation account.
check.feedback: The policy requires consultation with the State ADA Coordinator at MMB before a denial based on lack of financial resources. Reimbursement requests are made by agencies, not employees, and a supervisor's view of the budget does not settle the question.

cards.back: Signed April 1, 2019. Directs MMB to work toward a goal of 10 percent employment of people with disabilities in the executive branch and asks agencies for best efforts and plans. Confirm its current status before citing it.
Under Minnesota Statutes section 4.035, subdivision 3, an order expires 90 days after the governor who issued it leaves office, unless a statute or the order sets an earlier end or it is rescinded.

Minnesota Statutes section 43A.191 requires agency plans to include a reasonable accommodation program and to ensure hiring, placement and advancement opportunities for people with disabilities at all levels.
Employees choose whether to report a disability; they are not legally required to. Counts reflect disclosure, so they can change when people update records as well as when hiring changes.

EEOC guidance allows inviting voluntary self-identification for affirmative action if the invitation says it is voluntary, confidential, used only for that purpose and that declining brings no adverse treatment.

Minnesota Statutes section 16B.4805 lets the commissioner of administration reimburse state agencies up to 50 percent of eligible accommodation costs, to the extent funds are available. Check the current text.
MMB Policy 1433 requires an agency to consult the State ADA Coordinator at MMB before denying an accommodation for lack of financial resources.

Prompt routing, follow-up, budgeting, accessible tools, fair access to opportunity and a climate where disclosure is safe. Individual accommodation and employment decisions stay with the ADA coordinator and Human Resources.

aid.heading: State the goal accurately
items: Name the source and date of any goal you cite, and describe it as an executive-branch target.
Confirm with Human Resources or the affirmative action officer whether Executive Order 19-15 is still current.
Separate the order's goal from the statutory plan duties in section 43A.191, which stand on their own.
Never treat the goal as a reason to ask an individual about disability.

aid.heading: Read counts with their limits
items: Remember that counts come from voluntary self-identification and can change without any change in hiring.
Ask the data owner what a figure counts, for what period and how small groups are protected.
Send any self-identification reminder to everyone, explain the purpose and say answering is optional.
Keep accommodation and medical information out of any workforce analysis.

aid.heading: Keep people, not only hire them
items: Offer stay conversations to everyone and leave exit information to Human Resources.
Announce development opportunities openly and check that each has a clear accommodation route.
Plan for transitions such as a new supervisor, reorganization or new system before they disrupt access.
Route possible disability discrimination or harassment promptly through the established channel.

aid.heading: Run accommodation as a system
items: Forward requests promptly and follow up if a promised accommodation is late.
Know how your unit budgets for accommodation and how reimbursement is requested.
Make sure an update reaches the person if an approved accommodation is delayed, and ask about interim measures.
Ask the ADA coordinator for summary timeline information, not individual details.

sources.title: Executive Order 19-15: Providing for Increased State Employment of Individuals with Disabilities (Minnesota Legislative Reference Library)
sources.note: Supports the April 1, 2019 signing, the 10 percent executive-branch goal, the 2013 and 2018 self-identification figures, MMB and agency duties, quarterly reporting, the rescission of Executive Order 14-14 and the statement that disclosure is not required (lessons 1 to 4). The order's current status must be confirmed with Human Resources.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 4.035 (executive orders)
sources.note: Subdivision 3 supports the statement that an executive order expires 90 days after the issuing governor leaves office unless an earlier end applies (lesson 1). It does not say whether a successor will continue or replace an order.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes section 43A.191 (agency affirmative action programs)
sources.note: Supports plan duties on reasonable accommodation, hiring, placement and advancement, supported employment positions, accommodation tracking and retention plans (lessons 1, 3 and 4). Consult the current text for exact duties.

sources.title: MMB — My Personal Information in Self Service (January 2024)
sources.note: Supports the voluntary self-identification page, its stated purpose and the statement that employees are not legally required to provide the information (lesson 2). Screens and steps may have changed since this date.

sources.title: EEOC — Enforcement Guidance on Disability-Related Inquiries and Medical Examinations of Employees under the ADA (2000)
sources.note: Question 23 supports the conditions for inviting voluntary self-identification for affirmative action purposes (lesson 2). Federal guidance; check for later changes before relying on it for a compliance decision.

sources.note: Supports the roles of supervisors and ADA coordinators, confidential handling of medical information, the 30-day update, consultation with the State ADA Coordinator before a funding-based denial and agency payment planning (lessons 2 and 4). Last revised 2017; confirm current agency procedure.
